explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Ezra looks among the people and priests and says, "…I found no Levites there." (Ezra 8:15). Priests and regular folks are in the camp, but the Levites are missing. Ezra notices the empty spot, and that's where the next part of the story starts.

Close, but the priests are actually there. Ezra says he searched "…among the people and priests…" and "…found no Levites there." (Ezra 8:15). So the priests are in the camp, and the Levites are the ones nobody can find. Easy mix-up, because those two get named together a lot.

Not quite, friend. The leaders are around, because Ezra summons them right after he searches (Ezra 8:16). What he finds missing is the Levites (Ezra 8:15). He needs those leaders for the job of tracking Levites down.

That's right. Ezra sends his team to Iddo and his kinsmen with a message that they should bring ministers "…for the house of our God." (Ezra 8:17). Iddo is the leader at Casiphia. It's a short message with a clear request, and I respect that.

Not this time, friend. The message asks Iddo and his kinsmen to bring ministers "…for the house of our God." (Ezra 8:17). Back in my junk drawer days I read plenty of takeout menus, and none of them were this clear about what they wanted. Ezra's note has a plain ask, and the text says exactly what it is.

Yes, friend. Ezra says, "…since the gracious hand of our God was upon us, they brought us Sherebiah…" and the others (Ezra 8:18). He points straight to God. Ezra could have patted himself on the back for his good message, and he didn't.

That's a good guess, because favors do make the world go round. But the text never says Iddo owed Ezra anything. Ezra says the Levites came because "…the gracious hand of our God was upon us…" (Ezra 8:18). I'd be careful about adding a favor that the page never mentions.

Close, because King Artaxerxes does show up in this story (Ezra 8:1). But Ezra doesn't give the king credit for this one. He says it happened since "…the gracious hand of our God was upon us…" (Ezra 8:18). The credit goes to God.
Not quite, friend. Ezra says Sherebiah comes "…along with his sons and brothers, 18 men…" (Ezra 8:18). That's a whole crew, not a solo act. Sherebiah doesn't make this trip by himself.
Right, friend. Sherebiah comes with "…his sons and brothers, 18 men…" (Ezra 8:18). Nobody has to hum a lonely tune on this trip. And Hashabiah shows up next with 20 men of his own (Ezra 8:19).

That's it, friend. The text says Ezra's team brings "…220 of the temple servants, all designated by name." (Ezra 8:20). David and the officials had appointed them to assist the Levites. Every one of them is on the list by name, and I'd call that a well-kept guest book.

Good guess, but the palace isn't in this verse. Ezra 8:20 says they're "temple servants" who were appointed to assist the Levites. David and the officials set that up. It's all about the house of God here, not a king's household.

Not this one, friend. Ezra 8:20 says "temple servants." David and the officials had appointed them to assist the Levites, so their work was tied to the house of God. City servants would be a different job entirely.

Yes, friend. Ezra says, "…there by the Ahava Canal I proclaimed a fast, so that we might humble ourselves before our God…" (Ezra 8:21). They ask Him for a safe journey for themselves and their children, with all their possessions. A fast means going without food to seek God, and the text says they fasted and petitioned Him (Ezra 8:23).

I like your style, but this is the opposite. Ezra proclaims a fast, not a feast (Ezra 8:21). They go without food to humble themselves before God. My ovens would be sad about it, but that's what the text says.

Good thinking, since Ezra already counted heads in this chapter (Ezra 8:1-14). But what he proclaims at the canal is a fast (Ezra 8:21). It's so they can humble themselves and ask God for a safe journey for them and their children, with all their possessions.

explanations.answer: He had told the king his God is gracious to all who seek Him
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Ezra was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers because they had told him, "The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him, but His great anger is against all who forsake Him." (Ezra 8:22). That's the reason the text gives. I think I'd be blushing too.

explanations.answer: The king had already turned down his other requests
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess, but the text doesn't say it. Ezra gives his own reason: he had told the king, "The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him…" (Ezra 8:22). Nothing there mentions any turned down requests.

explanations.answer: He knew the king needed every soldier to guard Babylon
explanations.explanation: Interesting idea, but the text never says it. Ezra's reason is that he had told the king, "The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him, but His great anger is against all who forsake Him." (Ezra 8:22). Nothing in the verse mentions soldiers being needed at Babylon.

Yes, friend. Ezra says, "So we fasted and petitioned our God about this, and He granted our request." (Ezra 8:23). They asked for a safe journey, and God said yes. That's a short verse with a big answer.
Not quite, friend. The text says, "So we fasted and petitioned our God about this, and He granted our request." (Ezra 8:23). They asked, and God said yes. The fast didn't go unanswered.

explanations.answer: Silver and gold and sacred articles
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Ezra says he "…weighed out to them the contribution of silver and gold and the articles…" (Ezra 8:25). The king, his counselors, his leaders and the Israelites there had all offered it for the house of God. That's a lot of weight to hand over, so I hope those hands were strong.

explanations.answer: Spears and shields for the road
explanations.explanation: Good guess for a road with enemies, but no weapons show up in this handoff. Ezra weighs out "…silver and gold and the articles…" for the house of God (Ezra 8:25). The protection for this trip comes from God (Ezra 8:23).

explanations.answer: Grain and oil for the altar
explanations.explanation: That sounds like temple business, so I see why you picked it. But the text says Ezra weighs out the "…silver and gold and the articles…" (Ezra 8:25). Grain and oil aren't in this handoff.

Not quite, friend. Ezra says, "The silver and gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers." (Ezra 8:28). A freewill offering is something people give because they choose to, so nobody owed it. No taxes in this verse.

Right, friend. Ezra tells the priests and Levites, "The silver and gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers." (Ezra 8:28). It's given freely, not owed to anyone. That's a different thing from a tax bill, and anybody who's opened a tax envelope knows the difference.

Yes, friend. Ezra tells them, "Guard them carefully until you weigh them out in the chambers of the house of the LORD in Jerusalem…" (Ezra 8:29). Their job is to protect it all the way there. That's a serious assignment, and no snack breaks mentioned.

Nope, friend. Ezra says the silver and gold are a freewill offering to the LORD (Ezra 8:28). Then he tells them to "Guard them carefully…" until it's weighed out in Jerusalem (Ezra 8:29). Spending it isn't part of the job, and guarding it is.

Creative, but that's not what Ezra says. His words are, "Guard them carefully until you weigh them out in the chambers of the house of the LORD in Jerusalem…" (Ezra 8:29). Guarding it is the job, and the text doesn't mention hiding places.

Not this time, friend. Ezra 8:31 says the hand of God "…was upon us to protect us from the hands of the enemies and bandits along the way." The text says nothing about any silver being stolen. And in the end it's all weighed out in Jerusalem (Ezra 8:33-34).

That's right, friend. Ezra says, "…the hand of our God was upon us to protect us from the hands of the enemies and bandits along the way." (Ezra 8:31). Then it's all weighed out in Jerusalem and verified by number and weight (Ezra 8:33-34). No stolen silver in the story.

Yes, friend. The text says, "On the fourth day, in the house of our God, we weighed out the silver and gold and sacred articles…" (Ezra 8:33). That's right where Ezra said it was headed (Ezra 8:29). The treasure ends up at the place it was given for.

The Water Gate is a spot in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:26), but it's not in this verse. Ezra 8:33 says they weighed it out "…in the house of our God…" I think the Water Gate is a good place to meet a friend, but the treasure goes somewhere else.
Close on the king part, since he gave to this offering (Ezra 8:25). But Ezra 8:33 says they weighed it out "…in the house of our God…" The palace isn't the stop for this handoff.

That's it, friend. The text says, "Everything was verified by number and weight, and the total weight was recorded at that time." (Ezra 8:34). Nothing is left to guess. Counted, weighed and written down, and I wish my cookie inventory was that tidy.
A seal sounds official, I'll give you that. But Ezra 8:34 says, "Everything was verified by number and weight…" The weighing is how it's checked, and the total weight is written down right then.

Names do matter in this chapter, like the temple servants "…designated by name." (Ezra 8:20). But for the treasure, Ezra 8:34 says, "Everything was verified by number and weight…" That's the word the verse uses.

Yes, friend. The text says, "12 bulls for all Israel…" (Ezra 8:35). The 12 goes with "all Israel," and the sin offering has 12 male goats too. Same number showing up twice, and I'd say that's no accident of the text.
Seven shows up a lot in the Bible, so I get it. But Ezra 8:35 says "12 bulls for all Israel…" The verse does have 77 lambs, but the bulls are 12. That 12 is the number to hold onto.
Not this one, friend. Ezra 8:35 says "12 bulls for all Israel…" Forty isn't in that verse at all. The 12 is the number to hold onto.

Right, friend. Ezra 8:35 says the offering included "…a sin offering of 12 male goats." It sits right alongside the 12 bulls, 96 rams and 77 lambs. And the verse ends by saying all of it "…was a burnt offering to the LORD."
Not quite, friend. The text says the offering included "…a sin offering of 12 male goats." (Ezra 8:35). It comes right after the bulls, rams and lambs. So yes, the goats are there.

explanations.answer: Assist the people and the house of God
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says the satraps and governors "…proceeded to assist the people and the house of God." (Ezra 8:36). The king's edicts get handed over, and help follows. That's a happy ending for the paperwork.

explanations.answer: Demand tribute from the priests and Levites
explanations.explanation: I see why that sounds possible with officials around, but the text says the opposite. Once they got the edicts, they "…proceeded to assist the people and the house of God." (Ezra 8:36). Help is what they give, not a bill.

explanations.answer: Send Ezra and his group back to Babylon
explanations.explanation: That would be a long trip back, and the text never says it. Ezra 8:36 says the satraps and governors "…proceeded to assist the people and the house of God." Nothing in the verse mentions anyone being sent back to Babylon. Help is what the officials give.
